Estimate prevalence and its precision

Source: R/estimate_prevalence.R
estimate_prevalence.Rd

Analysis function: given observed counts, returns a prevalence point estimate and confidence interval. Three CI methods are available:

"wald" (default)

Symmetric unless an end is moved to 0 or 1. \(\hat{p} \pm z \cdot SE\). Can be too narrow for small samples or prevalence near 0 or 1.

"clopper-pearson"

Asymmetric. Exact binomial interval, via the beta distribution. For a simple random sample, its coverage is at least the stated confidence level, so it is usually wider than the Wald interval.

"agresti-coull"

Asymmetric. A Wald interval calculated after adding \(z^2/2\) positive and \(z^2/2\) negative cases to the data (about 1.92 of each at 95 percent). This moves the interval towards 0.5; the reported prevalence is unchanged.

All methods account for imperfect diagnostic tests (Rogan-Gladen correction) and clustered sampling (Kish design effect).

If icc is not supplied, it is estimated from the data (the observed variance between sites compared with the variance expected if every person were independent). Setting icc = 0 treats every person as independent; if people at the same site tend to be similar, this gives an interval that is too narrow.

Usage

estimate_prevalence(
  x,
  n,
  sensitivity = 1,
  specificity = 1,
  conf_level = 0.95,
  icc = NULL,
  ci_method = c("wald", "clopper-pearson", "agresti-coull")
)

Arguments

x

Vector of whole-number counts of people who tested positive, one per site (a single number for one site).

n

Vector of whole-number totals tested, one per site (same length as x).

sensitivity

Diagnostic sensitivity in (0, 1]; default 1 (the test never misses a case).

specificity

Diagnostic specificity in (0, 1]; default 1 (the test never gives a false positive). sensitivity + specificity must exceed 1.

conf_level

Confidence level, in (0, 1); default 0.95.

icc

Optional. Intra-cluster correlation, in [0, 1]. If NULL (default), ICC is estimated from the data. Set to 0 for no clustering. A supplied value is also used with a single site.

ci_method

CI method: "wald" (default), "clopper-pearson", or "agresti-coull". See Description.

Value

A list with:

prevalence

Point estimate of true prevalence (Rogan-Gladen corrected).

ci_lower, ci_upper

Confidence limits on the true-prevalence scale.

moe

Half-width of the interval, (ci_upper - ci_lower) / 2.

n_eff

Effective sample size, sum(n) / deff.

icc

ICC used: as supplied, or estimated from the data.

deff

Design effect applied (1 when there is no clustering).

Details

The interval is built in five steps: apparent prevalence, a design effect for clustering, an effective sample size, a confidence interval by the chosen method, and finally the Rogan-Gladen correction for an imperfect test.

1. Apparent prevalence. The pooled proportion of test positives across all sites,

$$\hat{p} = \frac{\sum_i x_i}{\sum_i n_i}$$

It is corrected for test imperfection only at step 5, so the correction applies identically to the point estimate and to both interval endpoints.

2. Design effect (Kish). Observations within a site are positively correlated, so a clustered sample carries less information than the same number of independent people. The Kish (1965) design effect scales the variance by

$$D_{eff} = 1 + (n_w - 1)\,\rho$$

where \(n_w = \sum n^2 / \sum n\) is the mean number of people per site, weighted by site size (the plain mean when all sites are the same size), and \(\rho\) the intra-cluster correlation (ICC).

ICC supplied: \(\rho\) is used directly, also for a single site.

ICC estimated (icc = NULL, the default): with two or more sites and an average of more than one person per site, the design effect is first estimated as the ratio of the observed variance of the site proportions to the variance expected under simple random sampling,

$$\widehat{D} = \frac{\mathrm{Var}(\hat{p}_i)}{\;\overline{\hat{p}(1 - \hat{p}) / n_i}\;}, \qquad \hat{p}_i = \frac{x_i}{n_i}$$

and the ICC recovered by inverting the Kish formula, \(\hat{\rho} = (\widehat{D} - 1) / (\bar{n} - 1)\), kept between 0 and

  1. \(D_{eff}\) is then computed from \(\hat{\rho}\) as above. With a single site, one person per site, or nobody (or everybody) positive, the ICC is 0. If everyone tested comes from one site, supply icc.

An ICC estimated from only a few sites is uncertain, and the interval then tends to be too narrow. In simulations with a true ICC of 0.1, 50 people per site and a prevalence of 0.3, a 95 percent Wald interval contained the true prevalence about 76 percent of the time with 2 sites, 87 percent with 5 and 90 percent with 10 (Clopper-Pearson: 80, 89 and 92 percent). With the true ICC supplied it was 92 to 95 percent. Supplying icc from other studies avoids this.

3. Effective sample size.

$$n_{eff} = \frac{n_{total}}{D_{eff}}$$

the number of independent observations carrying the same information as the clustered sample.

4. Confidence interval on apparent prevalence. Let \(z = \Phi^{-1}(1 - \alpha/2)\), \(\alpha = 1 - \) conf_level, and \(x_{eff} = \hat{p}\,n_{eff}\), the number of positives scaled to the effective sample size. Any end below 0 is set to 0 and any end above 1 is set to 1.

"wald" – the normal-approximation interval,

$$\hat{p} \;\pm\; z \sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}(1 - \hat{p})}{n_{eff}}}$$

For small \(n\) or prevalence near 0 or 1 it can be too narrow, and it has zero width when \(\hat{p} = 0\) or \(1\). For example, with 30 people and a true prevalence of 5 percent, a 95 percent Wald interval contains the true prevalence only about 78 percent of the time.

"clopper-pearson" – the exact binomial interval,

$$L = B^{-1}\!\left(\tfrac{\alpha}{2};\; x_{eff},\; n_{eff} - x_{eff} + 1\right)$$ $$U = B^{-1}\!\left(1 - \tfrac{\alpha}{2};\; x_{eff} + 1,\; n_{eff} - x_{eff}\right)$$

where \(B^{-1}(q; a, b)\) is the \(q\)-th quantile of a beta distribution, and \(L = 0\) when \(\hat{p} = 0\) and \(U = 1\) when \(\hat{p} = 1\). \(x_{eff}\) need not be a whole number, so the design effect can be applied; coverage of at least the stated level then holds only approximately.

"agresti-coull" – add \(z^2/2\) positive and \(z^2/2\) negative cases, then take a Wald interval on the adjusted proportion,

$$\tilde{n} = n_{eff} + z^2, \qquad \tilde{p} = \frac{x_{eff} + z^2/2}{\tilde{n}}$$ $$\tilde{p} \;\pm\; z \sqrt{\frac{\tilde{p}(1 - \tilde{p})}{\tilde{n}}}$$

5. Rogan-Gladen correction. An imperfect test inflates apparent prevalence through false positives and deflates it through false negatives. Inverting \(p_{app} = p\,Se + (1 - p)(1 - Sp)\) gives true prevalence,

$$p = \frac{p_{app} - (1 - Sp)}{Se + Sp - 1}$$

This same formula is applied to \(\hat{p}\) and to both CI endpoints, and the results are kept within [0, 1]. If the whole corrected interval lies below 0 (fewer positives than false positives alone would produce) or above 1, the function warns that the data do not fit the assumed sensitivity and specificity.

Margin of error. moe is the half-width of the corrected interval, (ci_upper - ci_lower) / 2. Clopper-Pearson and Agresti-Coull intervals are asymmetric, and so is a Wald interval with an end moved to 0 or 1; report ci_lower and ci_upper then.

References

MMS-SD Study Design Workshop. https://mrc-ide.github.io/MMS-SD_workshop/

Kish, L. (1965) Survey Sampling. Wiley.

Clopper, C. J. & Pearson, E. S. (1934) The use of confidence or fiducial limits illustrated in the case of the binomial. Biometrika 26(4), 404-413. doi:10.1093/biomet/26.4.404

Agresti, A. & Coull, B. A. (1998) Approximate is better than "exact" for interval estimation of binomial proportions. The American Statistician 52(2), 119-126. doi:10.1080/00031305.1998.10480550

Rogan, W. J. & Gladen, B. (1978) Estimating prevalence from the results of a screening test. American Journal of Epidemiology 107(1), 71-76. doi:10.1093/oxfordjournals.aje.a112510

Examples

# Single site / simple random sample
estimate_prevalence(x = 8, n = 50)
#> $prevalence
#> [1] 0.16
#> 
#> $ci_lower
#> [1] 0.05838385
#> 
#> $ci_upper
#> [1] 0.2616161
#> 
#> $moe
#> [1] 0.1016161
#> 
#> $n_eff
#> [1] 50
#> 
#> $icc
#> [1] 0
#> 
#> $deff
#> [1] 1
#> 

# Multi-site clustered data -- ICC estimated from the data
estimate_prevalence(
  x = c(0, 4, 0, 22, 25, 16, 12, 8),
  n = c(60, 80, 70, 100, 40, 60, 50, 90)
)
#> $prevalence
#> [1] 0.1581818
#> 
#> $ci_lower

#> 
#> $ci_upper
#> [1] 0.3010005
#> 
#> $moe
#> [1] 0.1428186
#> 
#> $n_eff
#> [1] 25.07848
#> 
#> $icc
#> [1] 0.2867281
#> 
#> $deff
#> [1] 21.93115
#> 

# Clopper-Pearson interval
estimate_prevalence(x = 3, n = 30, ci_method = "clopper-pearson")
#> $prevalence
